idiom_name: Enumerator::Lazy chain (#lazy) forced by a terminal, or hand-written reducing procs
implementation_notes: Ruby's eager Enumerable chain is the staged form; Enumerator::Lazy is the stdlib realisation of the pattern - it redefines most Enumerable methods so that map/select/reject/filter_map/take/drop_while chain by constructing another lazy enumerator instead of evaluating immediately, and evaluation happens only when a non-redefined terminal is called (first, to_a/force, reduce). Any Enumerable is a source, Lazy.new(obj) { |yielder, *values| ... } builds a custom stage from a block, and the destination is whatever forces the chain, so the transformation chain is independent of both. What replaces the classic structure: the lazy enumerator chain replaces a reducing-function transformer for iterator-to-iterator work - pairs of procs (->(f) { ->(rf) { ->(acc, x) { rf.(acc, f.(x)) } } }) give the literal transducer in a couple of lines when a non-Enumerable sink or a published transformation value is required.
pitfalls: Lazy chains always require a block: [1, 2, 3].lazy.map without one raises ArgumentError, while the eager form silently returns an Enumerator.
Nothing runs until forced, and forcing an unbounded enumerator with to_a/force hangs - bound it with first(n)/take(n).
Laziness moves when side effects and exceptions happen (at force time, not at chain construction), and a chain that is never forced does nothing at all.
Enumerator::Lazy re-enumerates the source on each traversal for re-runnable sources, and an external enumerator holds a Fiber alive until it finishes - a leaked enumerator leaks that Fiber.
